blogs.title: When “We Almost Need to Come Inside” Is Still Consent: Voluntariness at the Edge of Domestic-Violence Policing
blogs.description: This post would examine the Seventh Circuit’s treatment of voluntariness where an officer’s request to enter a home came after a reported domestic-violence threat and included the phrase that police ‘almost need to come inside.’ It would analyze how the panel distinguished urgency from coercion, why Lisa Coleman’s earlier refusal became central to the voluntariness finding, and whether the opinion subtly lowers the practical bar for consent in high-pressure welfare-check settings.

blogs.title: Consent to Check on the Children, Consent to Sweep the House? The Scope Question in Coleman
blogs.description: This post would focus on the court’s conclusion that consent to enter for a child-safety check necessarily allowed officers to move through the home, locate Jaison Coleman, and ask questions of the children. It would explore the opinion’s use of objective reasonableness under Florida v. Jimeno, the line between a limited welfare check and a broader protective sweep, and what this means for future cases where officers enter on a narrow stated purpose but discover evidence supporting a later warrant.

blogs.title: Body Cameras and Clear-Error Review: How Video Evidence Shapes Fourth Amendment Suppression Appeals
blogs.description: This post would analyze the institutional dimension of the decision: the court’s reliance on body-camera footage and its insistence that appellate review remains constrained by clear-error principles. It would discuss the opinion’s invocation of Scott v. Harris and Norville, how video can both narrow factual disputes and strengthen trial-court findings, and whether suppression litigation is increasingly becoming a battle over how appellate judges characterize recorded tone, hesitation, and implied meaning.

blogs.title: The Road Not Taken: Why the Seventh Circuit Resolved Coleman on Consent Instead of Exigency
blogs.description: This post would consider the significance of the panel’s decision not to reach the government’s alternative arguments based on exigent circumstances and inevitable discovery. It would explore the doctrinal and practical consequences of preferring consent over exigency in domestic-violence responses, including whether courts are incentivizing officers to seek conversational acquiescence before invoking emergency authority, and how that choice may affect future litigation over home entry, safety checks, and later searches.
